quote: At a low dose of EPI ([dose figure omitted]), mechanical hyperalgesia also lasted longer in GRK2+/ than in WT mice (Fig. 1C). In addition, at this low dose of EPI, acute hyperalgesia was increased in GRK2+/ mice.
proposed_wording: The two-hour figure comes from Khasar 1999 (PMID 10085337), which injected epinephrine intradermally into the dorsum of the rat hindpaw, in skin with no nerve damage, and reported hyperalgesia lasting two hours; that study reported a dose-dependent mechanical hyperalgesia, not a single epinephrine amount. The length of the window has been measured again since, in mice, after a single intraplantar epinephrine injection (Wang 2011, PMID 21514055): mechanical and thermal hyperalgesia lasted 3 to 4 days in wild-type mice and about 21 days when GRK2 was reduced in sensory neurons, and a second, lower epinephrine amount gave a shorter window in both genotypes, which the authors describe as a leftward shift of the dose-response curve. No study found maps the window's length across a range of epinephrine amounts in one experiment.

Wang injected epinephrine ([dose figure omitted]) as a single intraplantar injection into the mouse hind paw, not an intradermal injection into the paw dorsum as Khasar 1999 used in rats, and the 3-to-4-day wild-type window is the time course after that one injection, read by von Frey rather than by the Randall-Selitto test; so it is a single peripheral injection into hind-paw skin but not the same route or species as Khasar's. On the elements the claim says are absent, the paper matches all of them: an animal study since 1999 that injected epinephrine into paw skin and measured how long the hyperalgesia lasted, at a second, lower epinephrine amount as well as the main one, with a shorter window at the lower amount (Fig. 1 panels) and an explicit statement about the dose-response curve on PDF p. 7. Two caveats for the merge: this is two epinephrine amounts rather than a mapped curve and duration was never tested statistically against amount, so a strict reading of 'the dose-response was never mapped' would leave the verdict at narrowed; and separately the claim's own premise is wrong at its source, because Khasar 1999's abstract reports a dose-dependent mechanical hyperalgesia rather than a single epinephrine amount.

On its own, then, this abstract narrows the claim (its description of the source as using a single epinephrine amount is wrong) without refuting it; what refutes the claim is Wang 2011, which measured the window at two amounts (see the own-question entry for C090). quote: Furthermore, we observed no apparent loss in PGP9.5 immunostained peripheral nerve fibers in both the back and paw skins approximately 1 day after co-injection (Fig. 7). The number of nerve fibers in each optical field for paw skins, for example, ranged 18 –24 (mean ⫾ se ⫽ 21.3 ⫾ 0.7, in 9 sections from 3 animals) in the saline group and 19 –23 (21.6 ⫾ 0.5, P ⫽ 0.732) in the BLA-treated group.

The nearest injected measurement is a rat study of a single subcutaneous injection, in which PGP9.5-stained nerve fibres in paw and back skin were counted a day later and did not differ from saline; the arm that was counted contained an experimental adjuvant as well as lidocaine and epinephrine, and there was no plain lidocaine-with-epinephrine arm (Wang 2008, PMID 18806059). The only human measurement of a local anaesthetic's effect on those fibres remains topical: lidocaine patches worn for 42 days lowered epidermal nerve fibre density in healthy volunteers (Wehrfritz 2011, PMID 21530339).

Wang 2008 did examine skin nerve fibres with PGP9.5 and did so quantitatively - fibres were counted per optical field in paw skin, 9 sections from 3 animals per group, and the counts did not differ (P = 0.732) - but the comparison was a saline group against a group given the experimental adjuvant together with lidocaine and epinephrine. Figure 7 has two columns only, SALINE and BLA, and the legend names the injected side as the adjuvant-plus-lidocaine-plus-epinephrine mixture; no plain lidocaine/epinephrine group was stained, so the paper carries no PGP9.5 result for plain lidocaine-with-epinephrine skin. The species is rat, the route subcutaneous (the paper calls it infiltration anaesthesia and never says intradermal), the fibres counted were in the epidermis and dermis of paw and back skin, and the timing was about 24 h after a single injection; the haematoxylin-and-eosin sections, taken about 6 days after injection, covered epidermis, dermis, muscle and subcutaneous layer and were read by a pathologist. The claim's elements - repeated wheals, intraepidermal fibre counts, any local anaesthetic - are therefore still not all matched by any study, so the verdict stays narrowed, but the wording 'the one measurement of any local anesthetic's effect on those fibers is topical' remains too broad because fibres were counted in skin that had received injected lidocaine and epinephrine (alongside the adjuvant).

The paper does not count needle punctures or deposits within an episode, and it never calls the injections intradermal or wheals (the authors say 'intralesional'). Sampling schedule: six serum draws from an intravenous line (before the first injection, after the first stage, before the second injection, after the second stage, and before and after the third stage or the repair), over up to about 8 hours (maximum 7.8 h, mean 4.4 h), analysed by gas chromatography, with no sampling after the visit. No subject reached the authors' toxicity threshold. Alam belongs, with Sato 2022, in the 'single-session surgical repeated dosing' class the reason already names, so the claim stands as written. quote: We made measurements 1.5, 2.5 and 3.5 hours after the injection of the anaesthetic.

The claim is not refuted overall: Miller 1984 remains the only eight-hour measurement, and Klingenstrom's injection was subcutaneous, not an intradermal wheal, so 'nobody has done the equivalent measurement in a human wheal' still holds.

quote: Cmax values observed at similar time points were similar on days 1 and 10 for lidocaine, prilocaine, and the sum of lidocaine and prilocaine concentrations (Fig. 1), with the two-sided 95% CI for each difference between day 1 and day 10 values including zero

quote: Patients were asked standard questions each day before the application of EMLA. The first question was ‘Please rate the current intensity of the pain from your ulcer using the pain ruler’.

Daily application has also been studied in painful carpal tunnel syndrome (Moghtaderi 2009, randomised, open-label, against steroid injection), and repeated non-daily application in nerve-repair and vibration-neuropathy cohorts. Outside neuropathic pain, daily application has been studied in chronic leg-ulcer pain over ten days (Effendy 2015, open and uncontrolled, no patient described as neuropathic) and for four weeks as a wound dressing (Purcell 2017, pilot randomised trial).

No patient is described as having neuropathic pain: the words neuropathic, neuropathy and neuralgia do not occur, the pain is called chronic ulcer pain, and the aetiologies are venous, arteriovenous and vasculitic. quote: Presently, this pairwise meta-analysis of 10 studies pooling over 890 pediatric patients undergoing topical anesthesia with EMLA cream or amethocaine gel is the first and most comprehensive review on the topic.
proposed_wording: The withdrawal is administrative rather than a finding of error, and the 2006 analysis stands as published, but it is no longer a current Cochrane review. Later meta-analyses cover the same comparison in children: Pywell 2015 (3 randomised trials; first-time cannulation success, no significant difference) and Varghese 2024 (10 studies listed; child-reported absence of pain favoured amethocaine in the 5 studies reporting it, RR 0.58, 95% CI 0.41 to 0.82; first-attempt cannulation success RR 0.98, 95% CI 0.97 to 0.99, from 3 trials none of which was significant alone; no significant difference in child-reported VAS (4 studies), parent-reported VAS (2), observed pain score (3) or child-reported acceptable anaesthesia (2); study quality rated with an observational-study scale and no certainty grading). A 2025 network meta-analysis and a 2025 clinical practice guideline cover the wider question.

Pooled estimates, EMLA vs amethocaine, random effects: first-attempt cannulation success RR 0.98 (95% CI 0.97-0.99; p = 0.017; I2 0%; 3 studies); child-reported absence of pain RR 0.58 (0.41-0.82; p = 0.011; I2 20.2%; 5 studies); child-reported VAS SMD 0.43 (-1.46 to 2.31; p = 0.525; I2 92.8%; 4 studies); parent-reported VAS SMD -0.05 (-0.64 to 0.54; p = 0.478; I2 0%; 2 studies); observed pain score SMD -0.45 (-2.27 to 1.38; p = 0.405; I2 88.6%; 3 studies); child-reported acceptable anaesthesia RR 0.73 (0.34-1.55; p = 0.118; I2 0%; 2 studies). The review matches every element D068 says is absent (a meta-analysis of EMLA versus amethocaine in children having needle procedures, published after the 2013 withdrawal, on procedural pain and cannulation success), so 'nothing has replaced it' stays refuted. Limits for the wording: one pooled study (McCafferty 1997) is a laser-treatment study in patients over 12 indexed as adolescents and adults; van Kan 1997 is listed but enters no analysis; quality was rated only with the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale and no certainty grading was given; the paper does not cite the Lander review; and the first-attempt and acceptable-anaesthesia intervals follow the Hartung-Knapp method on two or three studies (ordinary pooling of the plotted estimates gives RR 0.98, 0.89-1.09, and RR 0.73, 0.61-0.87).
